name: The Three P's
oneLine: Crossman's three P's: permission to do something different, protection if it goes wrong, and potency - real standing to make that protection mean something.
whatYouDid: You noticed that telling Kabir "it's okay to say no" wasn't enough on its own, and gave him an explicit promise of backup plus the standing to make that promise credible.
confusion: People often assume permission alone is the generous part and protection is a nice extra - Crossman's point runs closer to the opposite: permission without protection can leave someone more exposed than if nothing had been said, because now they've been told to act, with no backup if it goes wrong.

fromBook.quote: Pat Crossman has suggested three P's that the therapist must provide in order to do this effectively: permission, protection and potency.

expand.definition: The three P's work as a set: permission (an explicit okay to behave differently than an old script says), protection (a real promise of backup while the person is still vulnerable to the old fear), and potency (the granter actually having enough standing that the protection is credible, not just well-meant).
expand.otherFraming: Steiner frames potency as needing to be commensurate with the power of the original injunction - a timid attempt at protection against a strong old fear won't hold, which is why all three P's have to show up together, not just the warmest-sounding one.
expand.tryThisToday: Before you tell someone "you're allowed to," ask yourself what you're actually prepared to do for them if it goes badly - if the honest answer is nothing, that's worth knowing before you say it.
